newsitem.title: UK: Russia has accord in principle on Soviet debt dues.
newsitem.headline: Russia has accord in principle on Soviet debt dues.

text.p: Russia this week agreed to settle the last major debt to the West it inherited from the Soviet Union in what analysts saw as proof of its keenness to remove any blot on its standing in the international financial community.
Moscow announced on Thursday that it had struck a deal in principle with Western creditors to restructure some $5 billion in uninsured trade bills.
"It essentially closes the chapter on the restructured debt of the Soviet Union," Merrill Lynch strategist Daniel McGovern said.
"They are serious about trying to get everything done before the end of the year," he added.
When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Russia took on the $100 billion owed to western governments and commercial lenders.
In the past year, it has wrung agreements out of nearly all those creditors to restructure the money.
The moves come just as Russia has borrowed on the international commercial market for the first time since the 1917 revolution, easily raising $1 billion at relatively low interest rates.
Earlier this month, Moscow reached agreemnt with the French government to settle outstanding Tsarist debts.
By next March, it hopes to have completed an agreement, reached after years of haggling in September, with commercial banks to restructure into new loans some $32 billion in leftover Soviet debt.

Analysts said Moscow is well aware that it has to take these steps if it wants to tap overseas markets again to help its difficult transition to a market economy, which is only now showing signs of growth after five years of retreat.
Moscow is expected to seek another Eurobond next February.
But UBS analyst Alex Mitcheson-Smith said Russia's overall debt was tiny compared with Latin American countries. "Russia will get investment grade long before Brazil, for example," he said.
Ironically, the latest moves to settle its foreign debt come as Moscow officials warn that the real threat to the economy is the mounting internal debt.
Widely respected deputy finance minister, Oleg Vyugin, told a conference on Wednesday that Russia was moving towards a situation where domestic savings were not enough to cover internal debt.
"It's akin to (U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan) Greenspan's warning about the euphoria in the U.S. stock market," Paribas analyst Stuart Brown said.
"It's a warning not to get too optimistic. There are bad tendencies that need to be corrected," he said, pointing to the need for Russia to deal firmly with its fiscal problems.
